summary.text: Bathymetry is the study of how deep the floors of oceans, rivers and lakes are, the underwater version of mapping the shape of land.
Ships measure depth by timing how long a sound pulse takes to travel down, bounce off the seafloor and come back.
Its charts guide vessels around underwater hazards and help with studying marine life and predicting currents and tides.

facts.label: Mapping gap
facts.value: Much of the seabed is less mapped than Mars

facts.label: Multibeam sonar
facts.value: Typically 256 narrow beams in a fan

items.prompt: A ship's sonar ping takes longer to return over one spot than over the spot next to it. What does that tell the crew?

options.label: The seafloor is deeper at that spot
The water is warmer at that spot
A fish school is blocking the sound
The ship has slowed down there

items.explain: The travel time of the sound down to the seafloor and back tells the equipment the distance to the bottom, so a longer echo means a greater depth.

items.prompt: Early sailors measured depth by lowering a weighted rope over the side. Why was mapping a large area this way slow?

options.label: The rope often snapped in deep water
Ships had to anchor before each drop
It measured only one point at a time
Sailors could only work in daylight

items.explain: Rope or cable sounding gives the depth at one point at a time, which makes it less efficient than other methods.

items.prompt: A satellite finds the sea surface slightly higher over one patch of open ocean. What is most likely beneath it?

options.label: A deep ocean trench
A flat abyssal plain
A large sunken shipwreck
An undersea mountain or ridge

items.explain: The gravity of undersea mountains and ridges pulls water toward them, so on average sea level sits higher over them than over plains and trenches.

items.prompt: Compared with the surface of Mars, how well mapped is the seabed in many places on Earth?

options.label: Mapped in far finer detail
Less mapped than Mars
Mapped just as well
Fully mapped since the 1930s

items.explain: Despite modern computer-based research, the seabed in many locations is less mapped than the topography of Mars.

items.prompt: A survey team swaps its single-beam sounder for a multibeam one that sends a wide fan of beams. What is the main gain?

options.label: It can see through solid rock
It maps more seafloor with fewer passes
It no longer needs any computer
It works only in shallow water

items.explain: A wide swath lets a boat map more seafloor in less time than a single-beam sounder, because it makes fewer passes.

items.prompt: Before mapping, crews measure how the speed of sound changes with depth in the water. Why?

options.label: To warn whales away from the ship
To find how salty the surface is
To correct for sound waves bending
To know how fast the ship can go

items.explain: Changes in temperature, conductivity and pressure bend the sound waves, and sound speed profiles correct for that bending.
